https://telex.hu/g7/adat/2026/08/07/infl.text: Menü Kereső A magyar infláció kakukktojás Európában Adat A Mol Mészáros utcai üzemanyagtöltő-állomása 2026. június 18-án – Fotó: Szigetváry Zsolt / MTI Hajdu Miklós Uniós összehasonlításban is rendkívül alacsonynak számít a ma közzétett, éves alapon 1,2 százalékos júliusi magyar infláció. Sőt, még az inflációs trendek is különböznek Magyarország és Európa országai között: míg a magyar árak egyre lassabban emelkednek, addig a kontinens többi részén a drágulás üteme változatlan. Számokban: az eurózónában júliusban 2,9 százalékra nőtt az infláció, ami alapvetően az energiaárak 10 százalékos emelkedése miatt következett be. Ezzel szemben Magyarországon a háztartási energiáért csak 2,3 százalékkal, a járműüzemanyagokért pedig 1,6 százalékkal kellett többet fizetni éves összehasonlításban. Tavasz óta csökken az infláció mértéke Magyarországon, míg az eurózónában 3 százalék közelében ragadt. Az eurózónás szintet a magyar árindex még az iráni háború kitörését követően sem érte el, áprilisban is csak 2,1 százalékig növekedett. Lényeges azonban, hogy ebben az időszakban a magyar benzinkutaknak az üzemanyagokat a kormány által meghatározott, nyomott árakon kellett értékesíteniük. Alulnézet: a magyar üzemanyagárak jóval alacsonyabbak , mint a környező országok többségében, noha a tavasszal bevezetett árszabályozás júniusban megszűnt. A Mol valószínűleg a globális árak növekedését csak némi időeltolódással érvényesíti. Ez piaci anomáliákhoz vezethet , de az új kormánynak is az az érdeke, hogy ne legyen drágulás, mert az üzemanyagárak alakulása átpolitizált téma lett. Tágabb kontextus: a júliusban enyhén emelkedő euróövezeti infláció tovább erősítette azokat a várakozásokat, hogy az Európai Központi Bank újabb kamatemelést hajthat végre. A magas olajárak az inflációs nyomást egyre szélesebb körben fokozzák, ami szintén indokolhatja a szigorúbb monetáris politikát. Igen, de: a magyarországi kormányváltással kapcsolatos piaci optimizmusnak köszönhetően tavasszal a jócskán megerősödött forint szintén fékezte az olajár emelkedésének következményeit. A Magyar Nemzeti Bank (MNB) középtávú inflációs célja 3 százalék, mindkét irányban egy százalékos toleranciasávval, így a mostani, váratlanul alacsony inflációs adat további kamatvágásokra ad lehetőséget. A forint most épp gyengülőben van, a piac ugyanis már elkezdett beárazni egy szeptemberi kamatcsökkentést . Ha fennmarad ez a tendencia , akkor a fogyasztók jobban megérezhetik az importált inflációt, és az üzemanyag-drágulást is nehezebb lesz megfékezni. Az alacsonyabb kamatok azonban csökkenthetik az államháztartás kamatkiadásait. Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! Legfontosabb Friss hírek

Source: AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura European officials have warned that Russia is intensifying hybrid attacks across Europe, including cyberattacks, sabotage and airspace violations, in an effort to weaken Western support for Ukraine. Speaking during the UN General Assembly, ministers from NATO’s eastern flank said Moscow was increasingly relying on covert operations rather than preparing for a direct military confrontation with the alliance. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Europe was experiencing a rapid increase in sabotage and airspace incidents. She argued that Moscow aims to frighten European governments into reducing assistance to Kyiv and called for tougher sanctions targeting Russia’s shadow fleet and military-industrial sector. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said Europe was already facing actual attacks, pointing to arson, explosions, drone incursions and alleged violations of Polish territory. Poland’s military said Wednesday that a Russian Mi-8 helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace from Kaliningrad. Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said Romania had recorded more than 100 incidents involving drones or drone fragments as Russian forces attacked Ukrainian infrastructure near the Danube and Black Sea. Bucharest has not found evidence that Romania was directly targeted, she said. Russia has repeatedly denied carrying out sabotage operations in NATO countries or planning a confrontation with the alliance. Despite mounting incidents, European ministers played down concerns that a conventional Russian attack on NATO was imminent. Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Russia did not appear capable of or preparing for direct military aggression against NATO while its forces remained heavily committed in Ukraine. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys warned, however, that Russia could expand pressure geographically through attacks on critical infrastructure and other hybrid operations. Officials said maintaining NATO unity, strengthening deterrence and continuing military support for Ukraine would be crucial, particularly as winter approaches. Budrys warned that Russia could intensify attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and use cold weather as another tool of pressure. European ministers also argued that strong NATO responses to previous airspace violations had reduced serious incidents, suggesting Moscow closely watches how firmly the alliance reacts. David Placher | For The Journal Gazette Placher Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Ask people what treasures they expect to find in a jewelry box, and most will name the familiar: gold rings, silver earrings or platinum bracelets, often set with diamonds, sapphires or other minerals formed underground. But what about amber? This warm yellow-orange gemstone is not a mineral, but fossilized tree resin from ancient forests. People have worn it for centuries, drawn to its distinctive glow and rich folklore. To learn why amber remains treasured, I went to Gdańsk, Poland. I planned to visit Gdańsk’s amber market and the Amber Museum, but dividing my amber experience into shopping and learning felt incomplete. Before seeing finished pieces in shop windows and display cases, I wanted to understand what it felt like to shape amber by hand. So I joined the Amber Workshop Tour, where I made my own piece of “Baltic gold” jewelry. Near the historic Chlebnicka Gate, a cellar workshop hides inside a historic townhouse. On charming Chlebnicka Street, my interpreter for the workshop, Sebastian Malyszczk, was waiting beside a row of bikes. We walked down a short flight of stone stairs and through a wooden door. Inside, amber gems were displayed everywhere, jewelry-making tools were spread across worktables, and finished pieces hung neatly on the walls. Jeweler Bogdan Koloss said “cześć,” a Polish word meaning hello. Koloss has been making jewelry for more than 40 years. Every inch of the workshop is used, creating an intimate environment that feels both crowded and carefully ordered. Malyszczk and Koloss gave me a brief overview of amber and warned me that counterfeiters sometimes sell imitations as the real thing. To separate genuine amber from fakes, Malyszczk explained, one simple test is whether amber floats. Koloss placed a piece of amber into water, and the low-density gemstone floated. Then he placed fake amber into the water, and it sank. Malyszczk also noted that many amber gemstones are translucent, though the color and clarity can vary widely. Malyszczk said amber once was valued as highly as gold. Its rarity and color both influence its value, with white, blue and green among the rarest and most valuable varieties. Koloss brought out a plastic container filled with rough pieces of amber still covered in the weathered outer skin formed by nature. I selected three pieces, and Koloss seated me at an old wooden bench fitted with a multifunctional polisher and grinder. My first task was to remove the weathered skin and smooth each surface. As the wheel worked against the amber, dusty outer layers gave way to flashes of honey-colored light underneath. As the amber brightened under the wheel, the rough surface gave way to a warmer glow, and I could start to imagine how the piece would look once it became jewelry. Koloss and I switched places, and he used a machine to drill holes in the gemstones. He worked carefully so the amber would not split. My finished product was three gemstones attached to a simple leather bracelet. Making the bracelet gave me a better sense of the judgment and patience behind Koloss’ work. With that experience in mind, I was ready to look at finished pieces not just as souvenirs, but as the result of a craft tradition still visible across Gdańsk. I went to look at amber jewelry on Mariacka Street, locally nicknamed Amber Street. The street is lined with jewelry shops, galleries and souvenir stands selling amber pieces in many styles. Close by is the famous Amber Museum. The modern museum has a pitch-black interior with minimal lighting, allowing the colors of the amber exhibits to stand out. The museum also displays amber gems with perfectly preserved fossils, a reminder of why amber captures the imagination. Many people know amber from the blockbuster movie “Jurassic Park,” where a trapped mosquito becomes the starting point for cloning dinosaurs. That image captures part of amber’s fascination: each piece can feel like a small-time capsule from a vanished natural world. After visiting the museum, I wanted to see the shores of Poland’s diverse coastline where Baltic amber can be found. I signed up for the Gdańsk, Sopot and Gdynia Tour, a scenic ride that traced the Baltic coast from working harbor to wide-open beach to modern seaside city. In Gdańsk, the waterfront carries the unmistakable rhythm of the shipping industry. In Sopot, golden-white sand stretches along a softer shoreline where amber hunters go after storms, at low tide or in the quiet of early morning. Farther north, Gdynia opens onto a lively, evolving coast shaped by maritime energy and contemporary city life. By the end of my Baltic Sea coast tour, amber no longer felt like a simple souvenir. It felt like a thread connecting shopping, crafting and studying with the character of Gdańsk itself. Here, Baltic gold is not only something to buy or admire; it is something to touch, shape and understand through the people who help keep amber jewelry alive. David Placher is a photographer and world traveler with ties to Fort Wayne. His travel stories appear on occasion in The Journal Gazette.
